title: UK Backs Two Non-Invasive Tests to Cut Nine-Year Endometriosis Diagnosis Wait
excerpt: NICE recommends Endotest and EndoSure for NHS primary care use, potentially ending the invasive surgery requirement that has left millions waiting years for answers.
body:
• UK health body NICE has recommended two non-invasive tests — Endotest and EndoSure — for NHS use to speed up endometriosis diagnosis in primary care
  • The average diagnosis time in the UK stands at 9 years and 4 months, rising to 11 years for women from ethnically diverse communities
  • Both technologies will be funded through core NHS funding during a three-year evidence collection period, with final guidance expected by October 2026

Two new non-invasive diagnostic technologies could dramatically reduce the years-long wait for an endometriosis diagnosis in the UK, after the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommended their use in NHS primary care settings.

NICE's draft early use healthtech guidance backs Endotest and EndoSure — two devices that can identify endometriosis without surgery, ultrasound expertise, or referral to specialist centres. The guidance recommends a three-year period of NHS-funded use while additional evidence on their accuracy is gathered, according to Nursing Times.

How the Tests Work

The two technologies take fundamentally different approaches. Endotest analyses a saliva sample for tiny biological markers called microRNAs, which can indicate whether endometriosis is likely present. The sample is collected and sent to a laboratory, with results returned to the treating clinician.

EndoSure measures electrical signals in the gut using sensor pads placed on the abdomen. Patients fast for six to eight hours beforehand, then drink water during the 45-minute test to help the device record gut activity. Results are available immediately after the procedure.

Neither technology has yet been proven accurate in primary care settings specifically, but evidence submitted to NICE suggests they are more accurate than transvaginal ultrasound performed in primary care — currently the only diagnostic tool available at that level. A third technology, DotEndo, was evaluated but requires further research before NICE can recommend it.

A Nine-Year Wait for Answers

Endometriosis — a condition in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus — affects roughly one in ten women of reproductive age. Until now, the only definitive diagnostic method was laparoscopy, an invasive surgical procedure carried out under general anaesthetic in secondary or tertiary care centres.

The consequences of that bottleneck are stark. In a survey of over 10,000 women by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Endometriosis, more than half reported visiting their GP over ten times before receiving a diagnosis, and more than half attended emergency departments because of their symptoms.

"A diagnosis of endometriosis can for some women take the best part of a decade, with the UK average standing at nine years and four months, and rising to 11 years for those from ethnically diverse communities. That delay means living with chronic pelvic pain that affects daily life, relationships and work."

— Dr Anastasia Chalkidou, Healthtech Programme Director at NICE

Real Patients, Real Impact

Simran Chavda, 15, from Huddersfield began experiencing severe pelvic pain at age 13. Repeated GP visits and A&E attendances failed to identify the cause, with clinicians suggesting irritable bowel syndrome. A non-invasive diagnostic test finally confirmed widespread endometriosis.

Her mother Sharan Uppal, herself a GP, described the experience of hitting roadblocks. "I lost count of how many times I took Simran to the GP. We ended up in A&E three or four times, spending over 10 hours on one occasion," she told NICE. "When the test came back strongly positive, it gave me the empowerment to go back to our GP and push for a referral."

Ami Robertson, 23, a Pilates instructor from Glasgow, waited from age 16 for her diagnosis. "I spent years being told my pain was something else entirely. I started to doubt myself, wondering if it was all in my head," she said.

What It Means for South Asian Women

Dr Chalkidou's reference to the 11-year average diagnosis time for women from ethnically diverse communities is particularly relevant for the South Asian diaspora in the UK. Cultural taboos around menstrual health, language barriers in clinical settings, and documented disparities in how pain is assessed across ethnic groups have all contributed to even longer diagnostic delays for these women.

Dr Gail Busby, a consultant gynaecologist at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, framed the broader systemic benefit. "An earlier diagnosis doesn't just change one person's life, it frees up appointments and surgical slots for everyone waiting for care," she said.

What Happens Next

The draft guidance is open for public consultation until 27 July 2026, with a second committee meeting scheduled for 12 August. Final recommendations, which may change following consultation, are expected by October.

During the three-year evidence collection period, both technologies will be funded through core NHS funding, with the companies behind them responsible for organising evidence generation activities. NICE will review progress annually before deciding whether the devices can be adopted for routine use.

Emma Cox, CEO of Endometriosis UK, welcomed the announcement but stressed that access to new tests must come with better training. "Availability of these new tests needs to go hand in hand with education of GPs and Practice Nurses to ensure prompt access to those that need them, and an end to pain and symptoms not being recognised," she said.
nri_angle: South Asian women in the UK face diagnosis delays averaging 11 years due to cultural and systemic barriers; these new primary care tests could disproportionately benefit ethnically diverse communities.
